title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Latches

Component which “remembers” a value until it is changed by a new signal.
Can be used to store \(1\) bit of data.
Widely used in digital circuits, e.g., for data storage, control and flip-flop circuits.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
SR-latch



Set-reset latches are the simplest type of latch.
Can be constructed from two NOR gates.
Two inputs, \(S\) (set) and \(R\) (reset). State is changed when a pulse (high voltage, or \(1\)) is applied to \(S\) or \(R\).
The output is \(Q\) and its inverse is \(\overline{Q}\).

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
SR-latch












Initial state: no voltage to \(S\) or \(R\).



\(Q\) shows \(1\), its inverse, \(\overline{Q}\) shows \(0\).
To reset, apply a pulse to \(R\).
\(Q\) set to \(0\) and \(\overline{Q}\) set to \(1\).
To set the latch, apply a pulse to \(S\).
\(Q\) is set \(1\) and \(\overline{Q}\) set to \(0\).
Applying a pulse to both \(Q\) and \(R\) is not valid.

text:
Exercise: SR-latch with NAND gates

Can you build a SR-latch using two NAND gates?

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Solution: SR-latch with NAND gates













A high voltage needs to be applied to both \(\overline{S}\) and \(\overline{R}\).
A pulse of low voltage will cause the state to change.
It is called an active low SR-latch.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Gated SR latch



We may only want the state to change if the latch is enabled.
This can be done by building a gated latch.
Recall that an AND gate is only true when both inputs are true.
So we add AND gates, creating another input, \(E\).



The state can only change if \(E\) has a high voltage applied to it.

section: Exercise: gated SR-latch with NAND gates

How could you convert your NAND gate SR-latch to make it gated?

title: Building With Logic Gates
section: Solution: gated SR-latch with NAND gates
text:
Solution: gated SR-latch with NAND gates













Connect a NAND gate to the inputs \(\overline{S}\) and \(\overline{R}\), we get \(S\), \(R\) and the enabling input \(E\).

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Application: switch bounce

Latches are widely used in electrical engineering as well as electronic computers.
When a mechanical switch is pressed, it may cause several pulses to be sent.
An SR-latch ensures that only one signal is sent, since subsequent pulses to \(S\) or \(R\) will not cause a change in state.

A gated latch can be used when state should only be changed when a device is Enabled.



E.g., an air conditioning unit may switch cooling on and off depending on input from a temperature sensor, but the unit should only switch on cooling if it has been turned on by the user.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
D-latch



0Data or transparent latches have two inputs: Data (\(D\)) and Enable (\(E\)).
The state changes to the value of \(D\) only when \(E\) signal is high.
When the Enable signal is low, the value of \(D\) is stored until the leading edge of the next rising Enable Signal.



A D-latch can be built from a gated SR-latch.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
D-latch


Built by connecting the \(S\) and \(R\) inputs of an SR-latch.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
D-latch (Alternative)

It can also be built from the NAND SR-latch.



This version is made from only NAND gates.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Flip-flops

Latches are inexpensive and easy to implement using simple logic components. 2
However, their behaviour can be unpredictable owing to a lack of synchronisation.
Flip-flops add a clack to synchronise their operaton.
A gated latch can be converted into a flip-flop by connecting a clock to the Enable input.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
JK Flip-flops



The JK flip-flop has the same behaviour as an SR-flip flop:

Reset: high pulse to \(K\).
Set: high pulse to \(J\).

If a high pulse is sent to both \(J\) and \(K\), then the state is toggled.
I.e., \(0\) becomes \(1\) and \(1\) becomes \(0\).











We will use this latch shortly to build a counter.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Counting in binary

We saw that digital circuits have two possible values: low (or \(0\)) and high (or \(1\)).
Everything (letters, images, sounds, programs) in a computer is represented by a number.
Numbers are encoded in binary using a certain number of binary digits (bits).
A whole (integer) number is typically represented using \(8\) bits (a byte).
E.g., for unsigned (\(\ge 0\)) integers, \(0 = 00000000\), \(37 = 00100101\).

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Building a counter
We can build a counter, using JK flip-flops, which increments an integer represented by \(4\) bits (half a byte; a nibble).

Start by adding one Push button as input and one 4-bit digit as the output.
The counter should start at \(0\) and increase by \(1\) each time the button is pushed.

text:
Building a Counter 2


The timing diagram shows how the values of \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_3\) should change.

title: Building With Logic Gates
text:
Exercise: build the counter

Add one toggle switch, this will act as the clock.
Add a High voltage.
Add one \(4\)-bit digit, this will display the output.
Add four JK flip flops and connect high voltage to \(J\) and \(K\) on all of them.
connect the button (clock) to the Clock input of the first flip-flop.
The output of the first flip-flop is \(Q_0\), the final digit. connect this to the \(4\)-bit digit and to the Clock input on the next flip-flop.
repeat with the remaining 3 flip-flops.

title: Welcome
text:
Intended Learning Outcomes
By successful completion of the module, you will be able to:

Describe the role of the different computer system components and their interactions
Explain how instructions are executed by a computer processor
Illustrate key computer architecture concepts such as instruction sets, memory hierarchy and data storage
Explain the role operating systems have in providing services and sharing


From the DPD The module’s lectures provide the fundamental aspects of computer systems and architectures, covering hardware, software and networking. The practical sessions enable students to reflect on the role of each computer component and understand how design choices impact data input, process and output. Independent Learning Students are encouraged to explore and understand different approaches hardware and software system design. Independent study and formative assessment also help students to assess an appreciate the evolution of micro-processors, hardware and operating systems. Intended learning outcomes
